title: King Cotton
objective: After this level you can explain how the cotton gin and the domestic slave trade spread slavery across the Deep South.
summary: Whitney’s 1793 gin made inland cotton profitable and raised demand for enslaved labor. After 1808, about a million people or more were forced to the Deep South.

cards.headline: A machine built to save labor ended up spreading slavery.
cards.body: In 1793 Eli Whitney built a machine to clean cotton. Over the next decades cotton took over the South, and slavery moved with it. How did a labor-saving machine do that?

cards.headline: The sticky-seed problem
cards.body: Long-staple cotton, whose seeds come out easily, grew only near the coast. The cotton that grew inland had sticky seeds that were slow to pick out by hand. Whitney’s gin (1793) pulled the fiber through wire teeth on a turning cylinder, leaving the seeds behind. Suddenly, inland cotton was worth growing almost anywhere in the South.

cards.headline: Why the gin spread slavery
cards.body: The gin sped up one step, cleaning. Someone still had to plant, hoe and pick every boll. Cotton became so profitable that enslavers demanded more land and more enslaved people to work it. A machine that saved labor at the gin multiplied forced labor in the fields.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: the gin saved work at one step. Planting and picking still took people, so slavery grew.

cards.headline: Sold south
cards.body: In 1808 Congress banned bringing enslaved people from Africa. Enslavers turned to a trade inside the country. About a million enslaved people, perhaps more, were forced from the Upper South, places like Virginia and Maryland, to cotton plantations in the Deep South. Many were marched in chained gangs, and sales split spouses, parents and children.

cards.headline: King Cotton
learned: Whitney’s gin (1793) cleaned sticky-seeded inland cotton
It saved cleaning work but raised demand for enslaved labor
After 1808, the domestic slave trade moved people south
About a million were forced to the Deep South

questions.prompt: After Congress banned imports from Africa in 1808, how did Deep South enslavers get more enslaved workers?

options.label: They hired newly arrived Irish immigrants to pick cotton
options.rationale: Irish immigrants mostly settled in Northern cities.

options.label: They ignored the ban and kept importing from Africa
options.rationale: The trade shifted inside the country instead.

options.label: They bought people from the Upper South in the domestic slave trade
They switched their plantations from cotton to wheat

questions.explanation: About a million enslaved people, perhaps more, were forced from the Upper South to the Deep South.

questions.prompt: Match each kind of cotton or machine with its description.

pairs.right: wire teeth on a turning cylinder

questions.explanation: Long-staple cotton grew only near the coast. The cotton that grew inland had sticky seeds, and Whitney’s gin pulled the fiber through wire teeth on a turning cylinder.

questions.prompt: Tobacco in early Virginia and cotton after 1793 had what in common?

options.label: Both were first grown by the Cherokee
A profitable crop drove a hunger for more land
Both were cleaned by Whitney’s gin
Both were banned by Congress in 1808
options.rationale: Congress banned the African slave trade, not crops.

questions.explanation: Tobacco pushed Virginia’s settlers onto Native land; cotton drove demand for land and enslaved people.
